chapters.title: Chapter 1: What a Trade War Actually Is

lessons.title: Why Countries Turn to Protectionism: The Economics Behind Trade Wars

children.text: You now know the tools (tariffs, sanctions, currency policy) and you have seen them used at scale in the 2018-19 US-China trade war. The question this lesson answers is simpler and older: if free trade genuinely makes both sides richer, why do governments keep reaching for protectionism anyway? The honest answer is that it is rarely pure economics. It is usually economics mixed with politics, national security, and a fair amount of domestic pressure.
The Baseline: Why Free Trade Should Win

markDefs.definition: The idea that a country should specialize in producing whatever it makes at the lowest opportunity cost relative to other goods, and trade for the rest, even if it could technically produce everything more efficiently than its trading partner.

children.text: The economic case for free trade rests on

, the two-century-old idea from David Ricardo that countries gain by specializing in what they produce relatively efficiently and trading for the rest, rather than trying to make everything themselves. By this logic, tariffs are close to a self-inflicted wound: they raise prices for your own consumers and businesses, shield inefficient producers from competition, and invite retaliation that hurts your exporters too. Most economists' baseline view is that free trade raises total output; the argument is almost never about whether protectionism has a cost, it is about whether that cost is worth paying for something else.

cards.definition: Shielding a young domestic industry from foreign competition until it grows efficient enough to compete on its own. Classic example: South Korea protected its steel and shipbuilding sectors through the 1960s and 70s, and those industries grew into globally competitive firms within a generation.

Some industries, semiconductors, defense hardware, energy, are treated as too critical to depend on rivals for. This was the stated justification behind the US Section 232 steel and aluminum tariffs, and it is the logic behind India's push for domestic semiconductor and defense manufacturing under Atmanirbhar Bharat.

A politically popular but economically contested rationale: raise tariffs to shrink the gap between what a country imports and exports. Most economists argue a trade deficit largely reflects a country's savings-investment balance, not unfair trade practices, and that tariffs alone rarely close it.

Import-competing industries, steelworkers, farmers, manufacturers, are concentrated, visible, and organized. The benefit of cheaper imports is spread thinly across millions of consumers who rarely lobby for free trade. Concentrated losers versus diffuse winners is why protectionism is often good politics even when it is poor economics.

children.text: The textbook cautionary tale is the US Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which raised the average American tariff on dutiable imports to roughly 59%, meant to protect domestic industry during the early Great Depression. Trading partners retaliated with tariffs of their own, and global trade volumes collapsed by an estimated two-thirds between 1929 and 1934. Economists still debate how much of that collapse was Smoot-Hawley versus the Depression itself dragging demand down everywhere, but the episode remains the standard reference for what an uncontrolled tariff spiral can do to world trade.

body.context: Estimated fall in world trade volume following the Smoot-Hawley tariffs and the retaliation that followed, widely cited as the standard cautionary case against runaway protectionism

children.text: India ran one of the world's most protected large economies for over four decades. Under the License Raj, roughly the 1950s through 1991, an import substitution strategy combined industrial licensing (you needed government permission to even set up or expand a factory) with tariffs that, on many product categories, ran well over 100%. The goal was self-reliant heavy industry. The result was also chronic inefficiency and a manufacturing base that struggled to compete globally. That system unwound abruptly in 1991, when a balance-of-payments crisis left India's foreign exchange reserves covering only a few weeks of imports and the RBI had to airlift gold reserves as collateral for an emergency loan. Finance Minister Manmohan Singh, under Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, used the crisis to cut tariffs sharply and open the economy.

markDefs.definition: A government scheme that pays manufacturers a cash incentive tied to their incremental output or sales in a targeted sector, rather than shielding them with tariffs alone. India launched PLI schemes across electronics, pharmaceuticals, specialty steel, solar cells, and other sectors starting in 2020.

children.text: India has not gone back to blanket protectionism, but tariffs on select items, mobile phones and certain electronics components in particular, have crept back up since around 2018, alongside the Atmanirbhar Bharat (self-reliant India) push. The main tool this time is different:
, direct subsidies tied to output rather than tariff walls around an entire sector. It is a narrower, more targeted form of industrial policy than the License Raj ever was.

columns.label: License Raj (1950s-1991)
points: Blanket protection across almost the entire economy
Tool: import licensing plus tariffs often exceeding 100%
Outcome: chronic inefficiency, ended in a 1991 balance-of-payments crisis

columns.label: Atmanirbhar Bharat (2020-present)
points: Targeted at specific sectors, not the whole economy
Tool: PLI cash subsidies plus selective tariffs on some electronics
Goal: build competitive capacity in strategic sectors like electronics, semiconductors, and defense
Outcome: still unfolding, judged sector by sector

body.title: Economic Rationale or Political Cover?
body.question: A government imposes a new tariff on imported solar panels, stating publicly that domestic panel makers need three years to scale up manufacturing to competitive cost levels before facing foreign competition. Which classic rationale is this closest to?
body.explanation: A time-bound tariff meant to let a young domestic industry reach competitive scale before facing full foreign competition is the textbook infant industry argument, the same logic used to justify South Korea's early steel and shipbuilding protection.

body.text: National security is the hardest rationale to argue against in public, which is exactly why it gets invoked for products that have little to do with actual security, steel, aluminum, even orange juice have all been covered by "national security" tariff actions at various points. When you see that justification, ask what the domestic industry lobbying for the tariff actually produces, and whether a genuine security case exists, before taking the label at face value.

Protectionism is rarely about economics failing to work. It is almost always a choice to pay an economic cost, higher prices, less efficiency, retaliation risk, for something else: political survival, strategic independence, or time for a young industry to grow up.

points: Free trade's baseline case rests on comparative advantage: both sides gain by specializing and trading, even if one side could produce everything more efficiently.

The four standard rationales for protectionism are infant industry protection, national security, correcting a trade deficit, and domestic political pressure, and they are not equally sound economically.
Smoot-Hawley (1930) remains the classic warning: a US tariff spike to roughly 59% on dutiable imports, met with retaliation, coincided with a roughly two-thirds collapse in global trade.
India ran one of the world's most protected large economies under the License Raj (1950s-1991), before a 1991 balance-of-payments crisis forced sharp liberalization.
Today's Atmanirbhar Bharat push uses targeted tools, PLI subsidies and selective tariffs, rather than the blanket protection of the License Raj era.
